query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior at intermediate temperatures can emerge not through conventional impurity or secondary-phase precipitation but via spontaneous nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries that locally reduces cohesion by promoting sluggish diffusion effects inherent to multicomponent mixing.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy (for example, a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy in a homogeneous fcc or BCC solid solution state)
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal aging at an intermediate service temperature for an extended period under an inert atmosphere
generation.conditions: Intermediate aging temperatures typical of service conditions with careful control of impurity levels; a controlled comparison is included with samples pre-engineered to incorporate Cr-rich precipitates at grain boundaries
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters of the principal elements (Cr, Mn, Ni) that form at grain boundaries during aging
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation leads to preferential segregation and nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries, with sluggish diffusion inherent to multicomponent mixing contributing to the process, which reduces intergranular cohesive strength and promotes brittle, intergranular fracture under load – a mechanism distinct from conventional alloys where trace impurities or larger brittle precipitates cause embrittlement
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples without engineered grain-boundary precipitates will exhibit reduced ductility and display signs of intergranular brittle fracture, while samples with pre-existing Cr-rich precipitates (which act as sinks for segregating elements) will retain greater ductility and show fewer brittle intergranular traits
generation.baseline: The as-cast or homogenized single-phase alloy that demonstrates ductile transgranular fracture behavior and balanced strength–ductility at room temperature
generation.boundary: Intermediate-to-high service temperatures (approximately 400–800°C) and loading conditions relevant to demanding engineering applications
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range and time scale over which nanocluster formation dominates, and the extent to which minor impurities may modify the segregation behavior, remain to be fully quantified

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples in a single-phase condition. One set undergoes thermal aging at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 700°C) in an inert atmosphere. The other set is modified by introducing fine Cr-rich precipitates along grain boundaries (to act as sinks for potential nanoclusters) prior to aging. After aging, perform tensile tests and fracture morphology analysis (using SEM, TEM, and atom probe tomography) to assess fracture mode and ductility.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (intergranular versus transgranular features)
Grain-boundary compositional analysis via atom probe tomography
Microstructural characterization via TEM/SEM for nanocluster presence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the untreated and engineered samples display similar ductile behavior and no significant nanocluster formation is observed at grain boundaries after aging, or if pre-engineering does not lead to retention of ductility compared to the untreated sample, then the hypothesis that nanoclustering of principal elements causes brittle behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. The ductility loss in metals and alloys can be related to the segregation of impurity elements at GBs (, ) and the absorption of hydrogen or helium (), which weaken GB strength and promote crack initiation at GBs, and the precipitation of second phases (intermetallic compounds, carbides, nitrides, oxides, etc.) at GBs (, ), which causes high stress/strain concentration due to the incompatibility of elastic and plastic deformation between particles and matrix. In contrast to carbides and nitrides, intermetallic compound–induced embrittlement at room temperature can be relieved at high temperatures because plastic codeformation between these compounds and the matrix can reduce stress concentration and, thus, delay crack initiation (). cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). B can compete for GB sites and reduce GB energy and, thus, repel the embrittling element Mn due to the decreased driving force for Mn segregation
